title: Drumming Interdependence
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells of returning to an informal West African drum class in the basement of Keith's small house after six months away. When Nomon offers ten dollars toward Keith's broken ski bindings, Keith answers, "I could not play the drums without you." That leads to the five hindrances, with doubt as the disco ball above two pairs of dancing partners: desire with aversion, restlessness with dullness. Nomon recalls teaching meditation to University of Washington medical residents, where thin Sunday attendance stirs a self-concern that blocks noticing the five people actually in the room. Kleshas, understood as coverings to study and clear away, take the place of adding more skills. Nomon ends on a second rhythm played fast, with the part half-remembered and the playing simply happening.

sentences.text: Last night I got to go do some drumming, an informal drum class.
There's a young man in Bellingham who moved here from New England.
He's quite wonderful.
He's a white fellow, about 35, and he's quite a skillful practitioner of West African drumming.
He's from Ghana, and Senegal, and a little bit of Mali.
When he first came to town a couple of years ago, he was really actively trying to create classes, to find a way he could teach drumming for a living, charge a little bit of money, and do posters.

I was trying to encourage him, because he's not only a really skilled drummer, but very good at breaking it down, explaining the music, and presenting a very step-by-step path forward, and at the same time really holding the line.
Very naturally and gently, he expects that the music will be very good, and very precise, and very well done.
He calls his little outfit Doni Doni Drums, and I guess that means little by little, little by little drums.

So he was trying to do this, but it really wasn't going that well from the point of view of attracting lots of students and getting enough money, so he took a day job at Trader Joe's, along with 120 other people in our community, it turns out.
Did you know that Trader Joe's has created 120 jobs?
So go buy more cookies.
Anyway, it's not a bad job, and I know quite a few people who work at Trader Joe's, and every one of them says, "God, I never thought in my life I'd work at a grocery store.
It's the weirdest thing, but it's actually a really good job."
So they all say that.
Maybe they don't all feel that way, all 120, but the five that I know do.
And then Keith, it turns out, my drumming teacher friend, has some other interests too.
He's also a quite skilled bird watcher.

I guess he didn't go to graduate school, so he's not an ornithologist, but he's a very good bird watcher, and so he also got a little bit of work doing field surveys of birds, and the drumming wasn't really going that great, so he stopped for a little while.
So I haven't been playing drums for about six or eight months.
I've been meaning to mention it in a Dharma talk because it's really been a wonderful practice for me on a lot of levels.
One is that I'm a beginner.
I really am a beginner.
We go around those [unclear: "end places"], and all the experienced students are always saying, "Oh yeah, I'm really a beginner," and you kind of know.
It's true, it is actually true, but it's kind of not true in a certain way too.
When I'm trying to learn a new rhythm in drum class with Keith, and I'm getting it wrong, and he's stopping me and correcting me, and telling me I'll only do half of it, it's pretty difficult.
I'm not doing it right.
And there's a part of my mind that tells me very insistently, "You can't do this.
You're not getting it right, it's slipping past you, you're trying too hard."
You're telling yourself, "Relax," and everyone's playing, trying to do it right.

But then, oddly enough, after going through that many times with different rhythms that he's introduced to us, after a while somehow you do relax, and somehow you are playing it in the right way, more or less.
You can't just space out, thinking, "Oh, I got it," and then do it wrong again.
You have to be very steady with your attention.
But having this experience, this arc of "I'm a dummy, I don't know what I'm doing," all those things, you're like, wow.
The learning is not that kind of learning of "I figured it out."

It's more that there's a part of my mind that figured it out, and there's a part of my mind that finally just got the hell out of the way, to allow the potential of my body and my mind and my heart to just come forth, naturally and with effort.
So it's an interesting kind of effort, a kind of working with that mind that says, "You don't know what you're doing."
So I've been meaning to mention that for a while, but then drumming fell away.

There were four or five of us that were going pretty regularly, but without Keith to call us up, and he's a pretty informal guy, too, he doesn't send letters or emails, he calls each one of us: "Ah, you want to go drumming tonight?"
Even if it's a regular night, he calls everybody.
"Yeah, yeah, Keith, it's a regular night, I'm coming."
Or, "Oh, sorry, I can't make it next week."
But Keith stopped doing that, and every one of us, to a person, pretty much stopped playing, and stopped seeing each other.
Somehow this little community just fell away, and we all have other stuff to do.
It's not like anybody missed it that much.
It's like, "Wow, I got my Monday nights back.
I taught a mindfulness class instead.
More time with my family."
I've got to watch a little more TV, relax a little more.
These are good things.
So it's not like the five or eight of us were going around town bemoaning our fate and asking Keith constantly, "When are we going to start again?"
We just let go.
A couple of weeks ago, he called us up again.
And last night I went, and instead of renting a place as he had been, it was in the basement of his very modest little two-bedroom house on Sunset.
It's the first home for himself and his wife, and he was very happy about this little house.
To my eyes it looked a little dingy, but he was very happy, so I tried to appreciate that.
Very small.
We went into his basement, and there were five of us, or six of us.
Even though we had not played together in six months, somehow it really was wonderful.
We had stuff to learn, and he had to stop us, and we had to figure out our parts and relearn some things.
But somehow we were really playing, and it was a wonderful feeling, a real feeling of connection.
It was more casual too, being in his house.
Then we drummed for two hours, which was the agreement he had with his neighbors.
He wisely talked to his neighbors ahead of time, said he would stop at eight, so we did stop at eight.
We went into his kitchen, a little teeny kitchen, five or six of us in it, and we drank beer, and we were hanging out and talking.
Then I got up, and he said that he had broken his ski bindings.
He went skiing and his bindings broke.
I thought, "Oh, this is a perfect excuse to give him some money."
Because he hadn't said, "This is a class, you need to pay."
There were no business arrangements.
He just called us up, we went to his house, and we're having a wonderful time.
And yet he clearly was the center of this group and was teaching us.
He had written parts out on his little whiteboard, and he had stopped us and simplified the rhythm when there was one part we couldn't figure out.
He said something about his ski bindings, so I whipped out a ten dollar bill and I was handing it to him.
"Oh, we all want to help you with your ski bindings."
And he said, "No, no, no.
You're like my family now.
And I could not play the drums without you.
I could not play the drums without you."
Which is true, because it's an ensemble form of music.
He can't be the lead djembe player without me playing the big dum-dum drum, which is a big deep drum, with the bell and the ding-da-dum-da-ding.
Without Aaron playing the medium-sized drum called the songbon.
Without Jen playing the little drum called the kinkanee.
Without two other people playing lower pitched djembes as support parts.
So without us he actually couldn't actualize his talent.
He couldn't actually be completely a good drummer without us, more or less beginners.
Maybe now we're intermediate beginners, maybe.
Compared to master drummers in West Africa, we're definitely like eight year olds.
Maybe.
And he's shown us videos of, it's a family affair, right?
There's a drumming family in the village, and everyone plays in that family, including the little kids.
Pretty male-oriented, I guess, though.
Little boys.
So I was quite touched by that, and I thought, well, isn't that interesting?
How much we need each other.
And then I was thinking about that when I came in tonight, once the sitting started, and I saw, oh, not very many people.
The thought arose in my mind.
Did that thought arise in your mind?
Like, oh, not very many people.
Where are all the other people?
And then a feeling of desire arose.
Like, I want more people to be here.
I noticed that desire.
And I noticed it seemed to be linked to some doubt.
There was some doubt arising.
Like, well, maybe.
We had just had a not horribly cheerful board meeting, actually.
We were looking at how few people have renewed their membership, and how we hurt people, all those kinds of things.
Once you're administering anything, you can find a lot of things to worry about, right?
So we were worrying about those things together.
And not terribly depressed.
We weren't giving up the hope, and we were making plans, and all that, but a bit of a feeling of doubt.
There was a little bit of doubt in the air.
And so then I'm thinking, with the five hindrances, right?
Doubt is like the kingpin on top of the system.
Doubt is up there.
And then doubt is supported by two pairs of dancing partners.
Doubt's like the disco ball, or the chandelier, maybe, depending on which place you're in.
Yeah, turning around.
Maybe it was the disco ball reflecting all these weird thoughts left and right.
So there are these two dancing partners, right?
Desire and aversion are really strong dancing partners.
And so I'm starting to wonder, when doubt arises, and if we study our mind, we might notice doubt arises often.

Does it ever arise by itself, or is it always supported by desire, wanting things to be other than how they are, or aversion, not wanting them to be the way they are, which are very closely connected?
Or is doubt always arising in some relationship to the other pair of dancing partners in our ballroom?
They must do a very strange dance, because they are restlessness and dullness, right?
It must be a funny thing, like who's in the lead?
Probably restlessness wants to lead.
Dullness doesn't want restlessness to lead.
So they have a lot of conflict, but they're dancing partners, so they can't get out of it.
And so then I was reflecting on a class that I was teaching at the University of Washington.
I'm in between classes right now.
I'll teach this again in February.
This is a class in meditation and stress reduction at the medical school.
It's designed for medical students who have finished the coursework and are doing the long internship that they do, called residency and fellowship.
Which can be up to six years long, you can believe that, unpaid internship.
And very intense and very busy.
And they're also still studying and writing papers and responding to things in their work and stuff like that.

And the other thing that's interesting about the residency is, I don't totally understand the system, but from what I understand, the people who are actually working in hospitals rotate hospitals about every month.
What happens on the Monday morning of your next rotation is you walk in the door, you say who you are, and you ask who your attending physician is, and that's your new boss.
You may or may not have ever met this person.
And it's not like the whole hospital comes to a stop while they give you a nice little orientation and you get to know each other and have a little chat or a cup of tea.
I don't think so.
It's like, gurneys are rolling by and the PA system is going and things are happening, right?
So you have to really land on your feet.
So these residents have a really tough thing.
And of course they're also making literally life and death decisions pretty regularly, right?
Diagnosing people, prescribing medications, making recommendations, deciding how to use their energy in this chaotic situation of hospital health care.
And so the medical school got worried about these residents, understandably, right?
These people are stressed out.
And it's been a very much a tough-it-out sort of system, a sort of six-year hazing in some ways.
So that made me think about our third mental factor, our third factor of awakening, diligence and energy.
So these residents have to have a lot of diligence, right, a lot of energy.
They have to stick to it.
And the reason they're starting to worry about residents and physicians, newer physicians especially, is that they're killing themselves.
That's why they're worried about them.
So that kind of was the tipping point.
I'm paying more attention to how these systems work.
Suicide?
Yeah, suicide, yeah.
They don't like to talk about it.
I don't think it shows up in the New York Times, but numbers of physician and resident suicides are growing.
And we know from people who are working in mental health in the universities that suicide among undergraduates is also growing.
And it's also not so well publicized.
So anyway, one of the administrators of the University of Washington Medical School who was worried about this was herself a very tightly strong, super capable, super smart person, as they all are.
The system selects for that.
These are very capable, quick-thinking, bright people.
These are our best and brightest in that sort of frame.
There's a problem with that kind of judgment, right?
But anyway, in that frame they are.
And so the assistant dean of the medical school, herself a very type A, intense person, was just working so, so hard in her job, working 68 hours a week, and she had a bit of a breakdown.
And in the course of having this little bit of a breakdown, she discovered yoga.
And she became a very, very diligent yoga student, applying some of the same qualities to yoga.
She was practicing every day, going to multiple classes a week, still working 60 hours a week at work, maybe 55 instead of 60.
And somehow she heard about the system of teaching meditation and stress reduction.
So she heard about my collaborator at the Veterans Administration Hospital, who is also a UW person, and she asked if they could have a stress reduction class.
So he got me to teach it.
Anyway, I've been teaching this class with the residents, and what's interesting for me is that their attendance is terrible.
Of course it is, right?
Why would you think otherwise?

You would think these people who are doing this incredible thing for years and years, working so hard in these rotations, would suddenly realize, "Ah, I can just relax, take charge of my time, go to mindfulness class every week, I'll feel so much better."
So their attendance is not so good.
They fill the class every quarter, 20 people.
You get 20 people signed up, and I show up on the first day, and there's probably 17 of them, pretty good.
A few don't show up for the first week, and we do some meditation, we talk about stress reduction and all these things.
And then the next week, there'll be about eight.
They're just busy.
It's hard for them to track adding anything in their life.
The only time they could figure out that it would even be remotely possible for the medical school residents to add this to their lives is Sunday afternoon.
So they're adding this on Sunday afternoon, when I think they're usually just collapsed on the couch.
They've got to drag themselves off of the couch and go to the conference room at the medical school to meet with me.
In the first class that I taught, I really was feeling very discouraged about this.
I'm like, well, where is everybody?
We know this is going to help them.
This is really critically important for them.
If people do come, you see really great benefit pretty quick.
They're a little disconnected from their bodies and their experience, as you would be, right?
That's a survival strategy, but right away you see them start to kind of unbend.
And the people who stick with the class write to me later about this big life-transforming thing, and they really appreciate it.
But I noticed my mind.
I noticed on the surface a sort of concern for them in the abstract: well, shouldn't they be here benefiting from this practice?
And then I noticed under that was self-concern.
I'm driving all the way here from Bellingham for five people?
I am a fully ordained Zen priest, and I've received extensive training in this at great cost.
In Massachusetts, I had to fly to Massachusetts.
I even flew to Massachusetts in the wintertime.
There was snow on the ground, it was dangerous.
And where is everybody?

What I realized about that was that the minute I got engaged with that thought, I was not actually noticing these five wonderful people who were in this room with me, who had made this huge effort to get down to the conference room and practice mindfulness.
So what is this mind, this mind that wants something other than what we have, that doubts whatever it is we're setting out to do?
What is that mind?
I was realizing all of this is really an important part of studying these factors of awakening.
We tend to think about things in terms of adding something.
We think that way, right?
If only I added another skill.
If only I could figure out how to play my rhythms right.
If only I could be a better person: a kind of adding.
And in early Buddhism they didn't think so much about adding.
They thought more about dropping away and removing and sort of clearing off.
The term that we now think of is afflictions: all the problems, greed and anger and desire and jealousy.
How many deadly sins are there?
Seven deadly sins.
The term in Buddhism that they use for those is kleshas.
It turns out if you translate kleshas really literally, it means something that's covering up your heart or covering up your mind.
Sort of a thought covering or a mind covering.
If only we had more mindfulness, more discernment, more diligence, more joy, more lightness and ease.
If only we had more concentration.
If only we had more wisdom, then everything would be better.
And if we had more of this stuff, we could overload, overwhelm all those things we don't like, right?
Maybe doubt would just be smooshed out of my life if I had a lot of good, solid mindfulness, discernment, diligence, joy, lightness and ease, concentration and wisdom.
If I really had all those things, if I really studied this and practiced hard, maybe it would push all that away.
And I think in early Buddhism they didn't really think that way.
I don't think the Buddha really thought about it that way.
I think they thought about it more like: really study your doubt.
Notice desire.
Feel it.
Watch it arise.
Watch it pass away.
And when you are free from that and free in that, and you're able to allow it not to grab hold of your mind, then naturally there's joy.
Then naturally joy arises.
When we played two different songs last night in drum class, one we did very carefully, and Keith had to stop us a bunch of times.
We did that for about an hour, an hour and ten, twenty minutes.
And then he whipped up this other rhythm, which maybe is an easier rhythm, I don't know, but he just said, "Okay, remember the part, let's just play!"
And we just played it, and we played it fast, and I couldn't really remember the part.
I looked on a little sheet, and I don't know if I was doing exactly what was on the sheet, but I was doing a version of it, and I was there just in the doing of it.
This was actually what I was going to talk about: I was going to read to you about the traditional system of Zen training in Japan.
I may be able to do that another night, because I'm still contemplating this mental factor of diligence and energy.
The system of Zen training in Japan is important too, because somehow we've inherited something from it.
It seems that we wouldn't have Zen here in this place in this time if people had not done the usual training in Japan, and yet we don't practice exactly like them either.
I have a nice autobiography I'll read to you from another time, by a Zen teacher named—and it's an autobiography about his training.
He was born in the 30s, so he did most of his training really post-war in Japan, and it's very intense, very diligent, very hard working.
So maybe we'll contemplate some of his stories another night.
Because of this topic of doubt, and how we need each other, and whatever it is that emerges from that, it feels so important.
We can't wallpaper over this stuff anymore.
We can't just be nice to ourselves and others and just smile even when we're actually not smiling inside.
We need to notice that dance in the ballroom, which is a part of our life, and how can we ever be free of that and allow joy and allow wisdom and concentration to arise?
We don't like that message.
We don't like being reminded of the darker side of life.
We would like to be happy and not worry.
That's a great song.
So I guess that's my talk for today.
Thank you very much.
